webTitle: Morning Mail: Woolworths increased prices during ‘freeze’; Abbott weighs in on Hastie cartoon; and turning the algorithm off

fields.headline: Morning Mail: Woolworths increased prices during ‘freeze’; Abbott weighs in on Hastie cartoon; and turning the algorithm off
fields.trailText: Cost of chicken fillets, potatoes and donuts rose during supermarket giant’s three-month promotion; former PM calls on One Nation to remove ‘offensive’ animated series; Caitlin Cassidy tries to travel back to 2012
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Woolworths raised prices for popular items – including a 33% mark-up on chicken fillets – within days of promising to freeze prices on 300 “family staples” for three months to help customers with the cost of living. Tony Abbott has joined in widespread condemnation of an “offensive” cartoon posted on social media by One Nation. And our reporter Caitlin Cassidy explores what it’s like to turn the algorithm off. Australia Brain freeze: The southern hemisphere’s only cryonics facility, Southern Cryonics, is selling people “a chance of life extension” for more than $200,000. Experts say there’s no way it will work. Woolies counter: Pricing data compiled by CW Scanner and provided to Guardian Australia shows the supermarket chain increasing the prices of at least four key products after starting its three-month “Price Freeze” promotion. Hastie takedown: The former prime minister Tony Abbott has called on One Nation to remove a cartoon labelling the Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie a “traitor” or accept that it’s playing a double standard. Granted: Anthony Albanese is under fire after an invite-only grant program allocated millions to marginal Labor seats and his old local golf club. What went wrong – and is this sports rorts all over again? World 9/11 remembered: CIA veterans recalled the chaos and confusion as the attacks unfolded – followed by a “war on terror” that left the agency with a tarnished reputation. Global bond sell-off: Nervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation. Trump bucks: Donald Trump’s promise of a US$5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has sparked incredulity and accusations of bribery. Gaza documentary: Testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders on the secret systems used in the war on Gaza has been revealed in a new documentary film about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians. Full Story Alan Jones on Trial: Fierce loyalty, fiery texts and a parade of witnesses | Week 6 After a slow start to the week, the criminal trial of Alan Jones accelerated with a swift succession of witnesses taking the stand. Through a former politician, close friends and loyal associates, the court heard details of alleged indecent touching, scornful text messages and declarations of an “unbreakable bond” with Jones. Nour Haydar speaks to media correspondent Amanda Meade to unpack the cross-examinations, key testimonies and courtroom revelations. In-depth On the edge of the main highway winding from Hobart to Tasmania’s west coast, the concrete shell of the Royal Hotel stands like a spacecraft lingering on otherworldly terrain. One of the few official ruins in Tasmania, the old building is roofless, weathered by the elements – and has just sold for $300,000. Located in the ghost town of Linda, near Gormanston, the historic property was snapped up sight unseen by a Perth chef, Naiche, and his partner. Not the news Would Hollywood have brought Practical Magic back from the dead if the intervening 28 years looked more visible on Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman? An awkward question, as it risks subjecting their faces to the invasive scrutiny older female actors already endure. Their return as leads in their late 50s and early 60s should count as progress. Yet it reveals a condition of female stardom: age can increase a female actor’s nostalgic value, provided it does not show too clearly on her face. Sport AFL| Fremantle frenzy has turned to fear as the AFL finals straight-sets exit draws nearer. Cricket | England has batted Pakistan out of third Test with Ollie Robinson taking two wickets in the first over. Football | Benjamin Sesko has soared as Manchester United surged past Sabah Baku in a Champions League return. Media roundup The NSW premier, Chris Minns, is hoping to avoid a 2027 state election fought over law and order as frustration grows within Labor at escalating gangland violence in Sydney, the Sydney Morning Herald says. Labor’s flagship $75m anti-extremism program is failing to reform the vast majority of participants, The Australian says. A prominent disability advocate is furious with Qantas after a battle over compensation for a wheelchair that was broken on one of its flights, the ABC reports. webTitle: US supreme court again rejects Missouri maps drawn to boost Republicans in midterms

fields.headline: US supreme court again rejects Missouri maps drawn to boost Republicans in midterms
fields.trailText: Latest decision appears to set the stage for the state to use its old electoral maps this year
fields.bodyText: The US supreme court again rejected a push backed by Donald Trump to overhaul Missouri’s congressional maps in an effort to hand Republicans an edge in November’s midterm elections. Its latest ruling, after days of confusion, comes less than two months before the pivotal midterm elections in which control of the narrowly divided US House of Representatives could be determined by a handful of seats. Following conflicting decisions that spanned four courts, Wednesday’s ruling appeared to set the stage for the state to use its old electoral maps this year. The end result does not completely end confusion for Missouri’s voters, who cast ballots in primary elections using the new map, butwill vote in November on the older map. “The state, the election apparatus, had no business going forward with the primaries under that bill, under that circumstance,” said David F Walbert, a storied voting rights attorney in Georgia, who has argued voting rights cases before the US supreme court. “The problem that we’re dealing with today is 100% the result of the state machinery that created this.” At the behest of the president, Missouri’s Republican-dominated legislature redrew district lines last year to net one additional seat for Republicans in the US House of Representatives. The new maps carve up a district representing Kansas City, long held by Emanuel Cleaver, a Democrat. After Missouri’s governor, Mike Kehoe, signed new congressional district boundaries into law in September 2025, the legislation faced immediate challenges, including a push by People Not Politicians, a campaign group, which gathered more than 300,000 signatures to force a statewide referendum on whether to keep or repeal the new map. But Missouri’s secretary of state, Denny Hoskins, a Republican, sought to use the new map anyway. The Missouri supreme court certified the referendum for the ballot on 3 September over Hoskins’s objections, ruling the new district lines would not take effect until 2027 – after the referendum vote – and that the 2025 redistricting did not comply with the law. The legal argument over redistricting pitted Missouri’s court, which is “not exactly full of foreigners that are some kind of wild liberals from California or New York”, Walbert said, against state leaders auditioning for the president’s attention. The court’s unanimous decision speaks to the clarity of state law on referendums. The law “suspends completely the effective date of the law that has been subjected to the referendum”, Walbert said. The state attorney general, Catherine Hanaway, also a Republican, immediately appealed this decision. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who oversees emergency hearings from the eighth circuit, refused to stay the Missouri supreme court ruling on Tuesday. But federal district judge Stephen Clark made a ruling only minutes later, in a separate federal case, requiring Hoskins to use the new Republican-friendly map – compounding confusion over November’s elections. Hoskins then said he would follow Clark’s order, and a federal appeals court panel declined to block that order. On Thursday morning, Kavanaugh again ordered the state to comply with the Missouri supreme court ruling, blocking the new maps. “Today’s decision ensures Missouri voters will not be forced to vote under a gerrymandered map pushed through by the state legislature last year and then cynically imposed on voters by the secretary of state, in violation of the state constitution,” said Mark Gaber, senior director of redistricting at Campaign Legal Center. “Voters deserve to have their voices heard and to have fair representation in Congress. The Missouri supreme court unanimously affirmed that principle, and now, so has the US supreme court.” The Missouri supreme court meanwhile ruled on Thursday afternoon that Hoskins, the secretary of state, had been in contempt of court after continuing to use new maps that the judges had ruled invalid. But chief justice W Brent Powell also noted that Hoskins had purged himself of the contempt after declaring that the order by Kavanaugh had ended the controversy over which map to use in November elections, and would direct local election officials to use the 2022 map.

webTitle: US appeals court rejects Trump’s bid to restrict mail-in voting before midterms

fields.headline: US appeals court rejects Trump’s bid to restrict mail-in voting before midterms
fields.trailText: Court declined to ⁠put on hold ⁠injunction preventing the USPS from tightening rules around postal voting
fields.bodyText: A US appeals court has rejected Donald Trump’s attempt to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in voting before November’s high-stakes midterm elections, dealing a fresh blow to the president’s attempted crackdown. The Boston-based first US circuit court of appeals declined on Thursday to ⁠put on hold an ⁠injunction issued by a lower court judge last week, preventing the US Postal Service (USPS) from tightening rules around postal voting. The panel of three judges, nominated by Joe Biden, agreed with the plaintiffs that the president does not have the power to regulate states’ election policy. “Appellants have not made a strong showing that the district court erred in determining that the Final Rule is likely unlawful,” they wrote, making reference to a rule published by the USPS to implement Trump’s order. It comes as the US supreme court also considers Trump’s efforts to introduce new requirements curtailing the practice, which the US president has frequently criticized despite doing it himself. Back in March, Trump signed an executive order seeking to prohibit the USPS from delivering ballots to any voters not on a nationwide list of eligible voters in each state created by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The result would mean a limited delivery of ballots to only the voters on those approved lists. Democratic states and voting rights groups swiftly filed several lawsuits, arguing that Trump’s ordered changes are unconstitutional. Meanwhile, state election officials who run the elections have said there is not enough time to overhaul their systems to meet the new federal directives. Indeed, with the midterms less than two months out, some states have already started sending out ballots. The Trump administration has called its plans to limit mail-in ballots “commonsense measures” aimed at protecting voting security. Trump has called the order blocking those plans “unreasoned and unlawful”. Trump has repeatedly sought to restrict voting by mail, despite doing it twice himself this year alone in his resident state of Florida. He has falsely blamed mail voting for his 2020 election loss to Biden, while promoting baseless claims of fraud. The president’s order allows states to voluntarily use the new system. But as yet, none have announced they will do so. The USPS, for its part, has said it stands ready to implement Trump’s new restrictions, which would require states to give the postal service the names and barcodes tied to mail-in ballots for federal elections, if the court injunctions are lifted. However, it has also said in recent court filings that the technology needed to administer the president’s order is not even available. And earlier this month, a USPS whistleblower warned of “potentially catastrophic problems” if the agency were to try to carry out the order.

webTitle: James Talarico accuses Ken Paxton of ‘ignoring’ Epstein survivors

fields.headline: James Talarico accuses Ken Paxton of ‘ignoring’ Epstein survivors
fields.trailText: Democrats are targeting Trump’s relationship with Epstein as part of strategy ahead of midterm elections
fields.bodyText: James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Texas, accused his rival Ken Paxton of “ignoring” survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s sexual abuse, as Democrats seek to increase pressure on Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections. Speaking in Dallas, where Republicans are holding a midterm convention this week, Talarico appeared alongside one of Epstein’s victims at an exhibit that featured about 3.5m pages of Department of Justice’s files related to Epstein. “When did pedophilia become a partisan issue? When did holding sexual abusers accountable become controversial?” Talarico said. Talarico, who has emerged as one of the Democrats’ best hopes of winning one of the Republican Senate seats they need for a majority in the chamber, is among several members of his party appearing in Dallas this week, seeking to counter the Donald Trump-led convention. Democrats have made it clear in recent days that highlighting Trump’s longtime friendship with Epstein, a convicted sex offender, will be part of their strategy ahead of the midterms, and Talarico sought to loop Paxton into the attack. Talarico said survivors of Epstein’s abuse had requested to meet with Paxton, the Texas attorney general, but he had refused. “Our attorney general here in Texas has the power to get justice for these survivors, and he’s refusing to do so,” Talarico said. He added: “Ken Paxton has two choices: he can stand with these survivors and get justice, or he can continue to cover up Jeffrey Epstein’s abuse. The choice is entirely his.” The Epstein exhibit, which has previously been shown in New York, features row upon row of shelves holding all the files released so far related to Epstein. Critics say some of the documents released by the government revealed victim’s names, and that some material has been withheld. Speaking in Dallas, Sharlene Rochard, a survivor of Epstein’s abuse, said: “Questions remain about what hasn’t been released and why. Releasing only half of the documents is not transparency, and it cannot be where accountability ends. “I urge people to read the files, to follow the evidence, no matter where they lead. And when those leads reach someone wealthy, famous, politically connected, Republican or Democrat, keep following them, because justice that stops when it reaches power is not justice.” On Wednesday Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running against the Texas governor, Greg Abbott, visited the same exhibit, reinforcing that the focus on Trump’s relationship with Epstein will not go away. “It’s really incredible that we live in a country where the justice system is so broken at every level that there has not been accountability of what we know was extensive sexual abuse, exploitation that happened for decades,” Hinojosa said, according to Associated Press. “And that powerful people who run this country are still living their lives without having been held to account.” Elsewhere Democrats condemned Trump’s Wednesday night speech promising a $5,000 “dividend” to all US adults if Republicans win the House of Representatives and Senate in November. Beto O’Rourke, former US congressman and presidential candidate, told a roundtable hosted by Bloomberg News in Dallas: “I think people will take it for what it is – it’s a gimmick, it’s a bribe. It’s another promise that the president will be unable to fulfill … It adds to the stink of desperation that is emanating from that convention centre.” At a press conference in a hotel near the convention centre, Robert Garcia, a Democratic congressman from California, told reporters: “Donald Trump is a known liar. This is the biggest liar to ever serve in government, period. And look, the dividend is not happening. He promised a dividend on tariffs; that didn’t happen. He promised the dividend on Doge; that didn’t happen. He promised some strange dividend from Air Force One six months ago; that never happened. “There’s no one in the country that thinks somehow this new dividend is actually going to happen. What the American people want is the president to actually focus on lowering the costs of gas, groceries and expand healthcare. The president has done the opposite. He’s made everything more expensive, and so he needs to stop lying and actually get to work.” Madeleine Dean, a congresswoman from Pennsylvania, described Republicans’ first midterm convention as a failure. “I think you can take a look at the arena last night, you can see the empty seats,” she said. “He is weak. His approval rating has plummeted. His numbers on the economy: a disaster. His numbers on this war: a disaster. His numbers of the personal economy for everyday Americans: a disaster. This is a spectacle really laced with fear.” The Democrats also faced questions about their colleague Senator John Fetterman’s surprise appearance in a video at the Republican convention. Dean said she has known Fetterman and his family for years “but what we have seen in his service as a senator is something very different than what I got know around John. You can see in his work ethic that he’s just not present.” The congresswoman said she held a one-to-one meeting with Fetterman in his office a couple of months ago, but it was “a disappointing conversation” and “he was not listening to me”. She added: “I am gravely disappointed with John and that stunt … I will tell you from the ground from suburban Philadelphia, my constituents are livid. Those who went out and knocked doors for him are absolutely livid.”

webTitle: Global bond sell-off resumes as surging oil prices stoke fears about inflation

fields.headline: Global bond sell-off resumes as surging oil prices stoke fears about inflation
fields.trailText: Crude jumps above $107 a barrel amid concerns over Middle East conflict and out-of-control government borrowing
fields.bodyText: Nervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation. The cost of a barrel of oil jumped 6% to above $107 on Thursday amid concerns that advances by Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coast in Yemen could choke off Saudi crude exports. The global bond sell-off that has rocked markets in recent weeks resumed in response to the news from the Middle East – which came against a backdrop of escalating concern about out-of-control government borrowing. Higher oil prices, which had already climbed since hostilities resumed in the Iran war, are expected to drive up inflation, prompting central banks to raise interest rates and putting the brakes on economic growth. Donald Trump suggested on Wednesday that the conflict with Iran could continue until “immediately after” November’s US midterm elections, at which point he claimed oil prices would be “tumbling downward”. The European Central Bank (ECB) raised its main interest rate to 2.5% on Thursday, with its president, Christine Lagarde, saying: “We believe inflation will be longer lasting than we had anticipated.” “The conflict in the Middle East continues to ⁠generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an ⁠extended period,” she added. As Thursday’s sell-off gathered pace in London, the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds surged above 5.37% – the highest cost of borrowing since 2007 – creating a fresh headache for the new chancellor, John Healey. With less than seven weeks to go until Healey’s first budget on 28 October, higher interest rates on the UK’s debt-pile will raise the cost of future investment projects and eat into the Treasury’s fiscal headroom. At the same time, the prospect of higher energy bills as oil and gas prices rise is likely to intensify pressure on the government to help consumers to weather the winter. Unleaded petrol prices have already risen by 6p a litre since the start of September, according to the motoring organisation the RAC, while the prospect of higher inflation has prompted some banks to raise their mortgage rates. Healey has promised to provide a “breathing space” for UK households while also addressing the cost of doing business. In a speech on Monday, however, he also sought to tame bond market fears by committing himself to “controlling borrowing to bear down on inflation, and reducing long-term pressures on our public finances”. In the US, where Trump has promised to write a $5,000 (£3,700) cheque for every adult citizen if the Republicans win the midterms, Thursday’s sell-off pushed up the yield on 10-year borrowing to 4.92% – the highest since 2023. The cost of longer-term borrowing also continued to surge, with 30-year yields hitting the highest level since 2007, despite the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, intervening directly in debt markets on Wednesday. Bessent hoped to bring down yields by buying back $6bn worth of government debt; but investors appeared to respond by deepening the sell-off. Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at the broker Capital.com, said: “Ultimately, a sustained drop in long-end yields can only be achieved by genuine shifts in macroeconomic policy: either the US government pulling back on spending or the Fed lifting rates.” Policymakers at the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, will meet under its new chair, Kevin Warsh, to set interest rates next week. Markets are expecting a rise – potentially enraging Trump, who has repeatedly demanded rate cuts. In a TruthSocial post last week, the president said: “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change.” A plethora of UK data to be published over the next week, including on inflation, jobs and growth, will give an updated snapshot of how resilient the British economy has been in the face of the Iran war. In the first six months of the year, UK growth was the strongest among the G7 economies. This was despite higher-than-expected oil prices and the absence of hoped-for rate cuts. Bank of England policymakers will also meet next week, but are expected to leave the UK’s key interest rate on hold at 3.75% for the time being as they continue to monitor the impact of higher oil prices.

webTitle: Does Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ count as a bribe if we never get the money?

fields.headline: Does Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ count as a bribe if we never get the money?
fields.trailText: Trump’s promise to pay $5,000 to every adult US citizen if the Republicans win in November was only one questionable moment in a nearly two-hour speech
fields.bodyText: Hello, from the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, where on Wednesday night Trump definitely, definitely, did not try to bribe the American public into voting for his party in November. Speaking for almost two hours at the American Airlines Center, Trump promised to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections. The speech felt very much like a desperate last pitch to voters: the electoral equivalent of a dumped boyfriend offering to take his estranged girlfriend on a mini-break to Venice. It’s very important that even if the $5,000 offer might sound like a bribe – “if you do this for me, I will give you this money” – it is not a bribe; instead serving as a “dividend”, paid because of what Trump says is his administration’s “tremendous economic success”. The $5,000 non-bribe – inducement, perhaps – was the headline of Trump’s speech, during which the president was the liveliest he’s appeared in months. There were no surreptitious naps here as Trump rattled through some of his greatest hits (Sleepy Joe, Barack Hussein, Crooked Hillary) to the delight, initially, of the crowd. I say “initially” because this was evidence that you can have too much of a good thing. Even your favorite entertainer can go on too long. That was the case here, as an arena that wasn’t even full to begin with began to quietly empty after an hour and a half as Trump, becoming visibly drained by this point, leaned on his lectern and called Democrats “communist” for the 11th time. Earlier there had been energy from the audience, with the Maga base cheering and laughing in the way a crowd might will on a comedian who is fondly regarded, but way past his prime. They went wild for Trump’s bizarre character assassination of Ken Paxton, his handpicked candidate for Senate, who was the butt of a joke. Trump has invested a lot of political capital in Paxton – a flawed candidate who is running neck-and-neck with the Democrat James Talarico – so you might have thought the president would spend his time here lavishing praise. But this is Trump, who a) is just odd, and b) can never resist an opportunity to put another person down. “He may not dress right. He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Trump said of Paxton. He wasn’t wrong, but it’s not the kind of thing that will convince people to vote for the guy, although Trump rounded off the remarks with the claim that Paxton “is the greatest attorney general in America”. That statement is worth a fact check, and we should be skeptical, too, about whether Americans will ever get that $5,000. As the Bulwark’s Catherine Rampell pointed out, Trump has previously discussed paying Americans: a “Doge dividend”; $2,000 tariff dividends; and checks from Obamacare rebates. Those payments also were not bribes, but neither did they ever come to pass. webTitle: Trump promise of $5,000 for US citizens after midterms decried as ‘bribery’

fields.headline: Trump promise of $5,000 for US citizens after midterms decried as ‘bribery’
fields.trailText: Critics react to bid for Republican votes with incredulity and point to potential $1.2tn cost atop existing national debt
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump’s promise of a $5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has sparked incredulity and accusations of bribery. “If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000,” Trump said during the unprecedented Republican midterm convention in Dallas. “It will be called the Trump dividend.” It comes amid extreme concern over the US national debt, which exceeded $40tn for the first time in August. Speaking to Politico, Chip Roy, the Republican US representative from Texas, sounded skeptical. “Well – I would like to know how they would plan to pay for … back of envelope … well over $1tn,” he said. In the moments after Trump made the announcement, Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget wrote on X that “this would cost about $1.2 TRILLION in just one year. That’s more than ALL THREE ROUNDS of COVID relief checks, despite no recessions. The result would be a huge spike in the deficit, and almost certainly in the inflation rate.” The US has roughly 240 million adult citizens, suggesting the cost of $1.2tn. The federal government spent about $7tn in fiscal year 2025, with about $2tn taken on as debt. “The 10-year [treasury bond is] approaching 5%,” Goldwein said on Thursday morning. “Inflation is not under control. We spend more on interest than we spend on defense or on Medicare at this point. Social security is six years from insolvency. Just about the last thing we need is to borrow another trillion dollars to send checks to everybody.” Spending like this risked an economic sugar high followed by a recessionary crash, he said. But Goldwein was most concerned about what might happen if Trump’s gambit is effective. “If this works, the lesson for every future politician is going to be: if you want to win an election, promise a trillion dollars. And multiply a trillion dollars times the number of elections we have coming up, that is a recipe for bankruptcy.” Democratic political leaders reacted with blunt condemnation. “After making you sicker and poorer with his war, Donald Trump now wants to buy your vote with $5,000 in taxpayer-funded blood money,” the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said. “The most corrupt man ever to occupy the Oval Office.” The Democratic National Committee (DNC) pointed to Trump’s record on similar pledges, from $5,000 stimulus checks as a result of the work of the so-called department of government efficiency (Doge) to $2,000 stimulus checks from revenue from tariffs. “Donald Trump and Republicans are once again offering empty promises to Americans,” said Kendall Witmer, the committee’s rapid response director. “The only people reaping the benefits of Trump’s economy are himself, his family, and his ultra-rich elite donors. Meanwhile, working families get nothing except sky-high receipts at the grocery store and the pump, unaffordable healthcare premiums, and wages that aren’t keeping up with inflation.” The Bipartisan Policy Center has been tracking tariff revenue since Trump began raising rates in 2025. As of 8 September, the US has collected about $210bn in tariff and excise tax revenue in 2026. At a rate of $21bn a month, the US federal government would have to collect tariffs for nearly five years to cover a $5,000 payment, assuming every dollar of tariff revenue went to the payment, and discounting tariff payments refunded to retailers in legal challenges. Peter Schiff, chief economist for Euro Pacific Asset Management, said that Trump’s pledge had already begun rippling through financial markets. “Even though bond investors know that, even in the unlikely event Republicans retain control of the House, Trump’s promise to borrow over $1 trillion more to buy votes won’t be kept,” Schiff wrote in a post on X. “The promise itself is so reckless that they’re dumping Treasuries, sending yields to new highs … “Making his promise even worse, Trump referred to his $5,000 bribes as ‘dividends’, as if his policies had been so successful that the US now has surpluses to share. Instead, his reckless policies have produced massive deficits. Trump needs to send Americans bills, not checks.” JD Vance appeared to walk back Trump’s pledge, suggesting that the benefit would be means-tested. But the US senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, promised support for Trump’s idea. “I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” Moreno wrote on X.

webTitle: Jimmy Kimmel on RNC convention: ‘They’re very nervous about the midterms, and rightly so’

fields.headline: Jimmy Kimmel on RNC convention: ‘They’re very nervous about the midterms, and rightly so’
fields.trailText: Late-night hosts recapped the Republican event in Dallas and calls to ban Zohran Mamdani from 9/11 ceremonies
fields.bodyText: Late-night hosts roasted the Republican National Committee’s underattended “midterm convention” and attempts to ban the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, from 9/11 remembrances. Jimmy Kimmel On Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host opened with the news that financial disclosures revealed how Donald Trump gave his aide and “least secret admirer” Natalie Harp a $45,000 cash gift for the holidays last December. Harp “is the woman who praises him, shows him his iPad, keeps him distracted, and in return he gave her a wad of cash – like you do a babysitter, like you do when a neighbor girl comes over and does a diaper change,” Kimmel quipped. Trump also gave similarly sized cash gifts to two other young female staffers. “But I just want to say, before you rush to any judgment, there’s absolutely nothing unusual about an 80-year-old billionaire president giving the three young attractive women in his office 45,000 bucks each,” said Kimmel. “You’re the weird one for even thinking that, and shame on you.” Kimmel then turned to the Republican National Committee’s unusual “midterm convention”, a two-day affair in Dallas aimed at convincing Americans to vote for a party led by a deeply unpopular president who has led the US into an increasingly unpopular war. “They never had a midterm convention before, but Trump wanted one and so they’re having it,” Kimmel said. “The president, he’s hyping this. He’s saying it’s ‘the greatest rally of them all’. He said it’s ‘really hot’, it’s ‘totally sold out’, which is funny because the RNC had to hand out a bunch of free tickets to this sold-out event.” A large number of Republican lawmakers have also opted out of the convention due to “scheduling conflicts” and “not wanting to be anywhere near him right now”, Kimmel noted. “They’re very nervous about the midterms and rightly so. They are in serious danger of losing bigly.” They’re in danger, in fact, of losing a Senate seat in Texas to the Democratic candidate James Talarico, whom Kimmel will interview on YouTube this week “under unusual circumstances” after a Trump-appointed federal regulator “threatened” his show. The Daily Show On the Daily Show, Michael Kosta also checked in on the RNC’s rare “midterm convention”. “Everyone is going to be there,” he said before several clips of Republican lawmakers claiming they would in fact not be in attendance, for excuses up to an including a Wednesday night high school football game, “stuff” that was already planned and a “can’t miss dove-hunting event”. “Yeah, you can’t miss dove hunting!” Kosta quipped. “Eat lead, symbol of peace!” In other tough news for Republicans, JD Vance told a crowd this week that the country was about to “celebrate” 25 years since the terrorist attacks on 9/11. “Well, we’re not going to celebrate it, JD,” said Kosta. “‘Happy 9/11, everyone! I brought Rice Krispy towers!’ “We’re not going to celebrate 9/11, but we are going to commemorate 9/11,” he continued, “and one thing I always think about is how in the days after the attacks, President Bush made a genuine effort to defend Islam.” Kosta played a clip from 2001 in which Bush reminded: “These acts of violence against innocents violate the fundamental tenets of the Islamic faith, and it’s important for my fellow Americans to understand that. Islam is peace.” “Boy, we really didn’t understand how good we had it, did we?” Kosta added. “I mean, I’m not saying this man was perfect, but that was a full, coherent, non-racist sentence. Hindsight, huh? “The point is, back in 2001, President Bush was imploring the country not to lump all Muslims in with the terrorists who committed 9/11. Now it’s 25 years later, so how’s that going?” Kosta then cut to a news clip about a petition to ban the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, a Muslim, from the city’s 9/11 ceremony, while Sean Hannity and Fox News’s Laura Ingraham criticized his signing of a proclamation declaring 11 September a city-wide day of remembrance. “Look, I know nothing I say is going to convince the Mamdani haters, but if you ask me, the idea that 9/11 is about Muslims v America isn’t just wrong, it’s accepting Osama bin Laden’s vision of the world,” Kosta concluded. “And the fact that 25 years after 9/11, we have a New York-grown, Muslim mayor leading our remembrance proves to the world that al-Qaida didn’t win. New York won. “So yes, everyone is welcome at the New York ceremony, and I would be there … but I’m going dove-hunting and it’s can’t-miss.”

webTitle: Ryanair boss says airline will dispute account of passenger who said they were partially sucked out of window – as it happened

fields.headline: Ryanair boss says airline will dispute account of passenger who said they were partially sucked out of window – as it happened
fields.trailText: Ljubisa Karović suffered neck and shoulder injuries after the window broke during the flight
fields.bodyText: Ryanair has said it will be “disputing” that any part of a passenger’s body was sucked outside when a window on one of its aircraft broke while in flight. US investigators are examining the incident which left Ljubisa Karović, 61, severely injured when the window beside him shattered on a Ryanair flight from Greece to Germany in July. Karović’s lawyer said the Serbian businessman was hauled back in after his head and right arm were sucked through the window due to the sudden depressurisation. However, Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, said the airline would be “disputing” that account, telling reporters after the airline’s annual meeting in Dublin on Thursday that Karović was “certainly sucked towards the window, but he didn’t get out the window”. The European Central Bank raised interest rates by a quarter point, the second hike this year, seeking to tame an energy-driven rise in inflation triggered by the Iran war, as it warned that fuel prices could move higher. A relative lull in the conflict came to an end in recent weeks, and in recent days the US and Iran hit ⁠military, shipping and energy assets, sending oil ⁠back above $100 a barrel – now at $104.53 a barrel, but approached $106 a barrel earlier. Natural gas prices have also jumped today. The ECB responded by raising its policy rate to 2.50% from 2.25%. It acknowledged that even then inflation is expected to stay above the central bank’s 2% target through to 2028, in part ⁠because activity in the wider economy is more resilient than thought. The ECB decision and statement prompted traders to raise bets on further hikes, pricing in 60 basis points more of increases by the April 2027 meeting, up from around 51 bps before. As usual, ECB president Christine Lagarde stressed the ⁠bank does not pre-commit to any future moves. She told a press conference We have not debated at all any kind of future path. Markets do what they have to do and we do what we have to do - which is to provide price stability. Lagarde acknowledged ‌that gas prices could rise due to further supply disruptions or an unusually cold winter, in combination with low storage levels across much of Europe. We believe inflation will be longer lasting than we had anticipated. Aberdeen economist Felix Feather said: More important than the move itself is that the ECB has used this ‌meeting to acknowledge a stronger economy and a more persistent inflation outlook than it expected just a few months ago. Thank you for reading. We’ll be back tomorrow. Bye! – JK HSBC’s first female finance chief is to step down next year, amid a string of high-profile departures at the Asia-focused lender. Chief ‌financial officer Pam Kaur plans to step down in 2027, the bank said on Thursday. Under chief executive Georges Elhedery, HSBC has undergone a radical restructuring in the last two years. HSBC said its board has started to look for a replacement for Kaur, and will consider “both internal and external ⁠candidates”. In December, HSBC unexpectedly announced that interim chair Brendan Nelson would stay in the role permanently after a seven-month search for a successor to Mark Tucker. Since her appointment in October 2024, Kaur had been widely regarded as the top aide to Elhedery as he led a global overhaul to split the bank into East and West regional divisions, exited some markets and slashed costs to streamline operations. Edward ⁠Firth, analyst at KBW in London, told Reuters: Pam Kaur’s exit is a bit of a surprise but she has done a good job since being appointed in supporting Elhedery’s restructuring and selling off superfluous parts of the bank, the results of which can be seen in the share price. The HSBC share price dropped 1.5% on Thursday but is 28% ahead so far this year. The wider FTSE 100 index has slid 55 points, or 0.5%, to 10,614. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, is now heading towards $106 a barrel, as fighting in the Middle East escalates. It is now at $105.66 a barrel, up $4.41 or 4.3% on the day. British gas prices continue to climb, and are trading at the highest levels since December 2022. The front-month contract briefly hit 207.2 pence per therm and is now 206.81 per therm, up 4.6% on the day. European gas prices have also jumped. The benchmark Dutch front-month contract rose 4.1% to €82.53 per megawatt hour. Yemen’s Houthi rebels are making a concerted drive to take full control of the country’s Red Sea coast, claiming control of the key port of Mocha, in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years. Seizure of the coast would be a strategic disaster for Saudi Arabia and the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two chokepoints for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. Mark Wall, Deutsche Bank’s chief European economist, said about the European Central Bank’s interest rate hike, the second this year: The inflation risks may be rising and a further hike in December may be more likely than not, but the ECB still needs to tread carefully. The economy has been resilient over the last six months, but rapidly rising gas prices mean the negative supply shock is building. It will eventually hurt growth. The question is how much and when. Here is our full Ryanair story: The ECB is now expecting headline inflation to average 3% this year, 2.5% next year and 2.1% in 2028. The next two years have been revised higher from its June estimates. The central bank is forecasting economic growth of 0.9% for 2026, 1.4% for 2027 and 1.5% for 2028. The next two years have been revised up “mainly reflecting the greater than expected resilience of the euro area economy”. Referring to an energy shock, the ECB said: The outlook remains highly uncertain, with risks to the upside for inflation and to the downside for economic growth. The European Central Bank has raised interest rates for the second time this year, as widely expected, at it tries to bring inflation under control. Inflation has been driven higher by soaring energy costs from the US-Israeli war on Iran. Surging oil and natural prices pushed inflation to 3.3% across the eurozone last mont, far exceeding the ECB’s 2% target. Oil and gas prices have jumped again this week amid an escalation of fighting in the Middle East, with Brent crude now approaching $104 a barrel. Christine Lagarde, the ECB’s president, will explain the central bank’s thinking at a press conference in 25 minutes. A statement said: The governing council today decided to raise the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period. Ryanair boss Michael O’Leary said that the airline will be “disputing” that any part of a passenger’s body was sucked out of a window midflight. Oil prices continue to climb, and are above $102 a barrel now after the US and Iran stepped up their attacks on ships on Wednesday. On Wednesday, an industrial facility caught fire in Novy Urgengov in northern Russia following a drone attack, regional governor Dmitry Artyukhov said on Wednesday, according to Reuters – the first such attack on the country’s natural gas hinterland. EU gas stores are only 67% full, well below the five-year average of 84%. Analysts at ING said: This leaves the market vulnerable as we head closer towards the upcoming heating season. The sharp drop at the open is the market saying Primark’s turnaround is still a story, not a number. Like-for-like sales at Primark, expected down 3% in the fourth quarter after a 2.2% drop in the third, tell investors the recovery they had started to price in is not here yet. They cannot, on their own, justify the multiple a standalone Primark will need. Europe remains the problem, and that is half the estate. Home delivery in the UK is the right call and closes a long running gap. It will not rescue this Christmas, and the market has treated it accordingly. The longer term case still seems intact for patient investors: a decent balance sheet, a 2027 split that should surface value, and a brand that still works when the offer is right. This morning is a reminder that the City is no longer paying up for the plan. It wants proof on the shop floor, and it did not get it. It was a mixed performance from the rest of ABF’s food businesses, with growth across grocery and ingredients largely offset by continued declines in the sugar and agriculture divisions. webTitle: Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast

fields.headline: Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast
fields.trailText: Iran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widens
fields.bodyText: Houthi forces in Yemen are making a concerted drive to take over the country’s Red Sea coast fully, claiming control of the key port of Mocha in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years, bringing the Iran-aligned group closer to full control of a key shipping route. Seizure of the coast and some of the islands in the sea would be a strategic disaster for Saudi Arabia and the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two choke points for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandab at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. Observers have said a reduction in hostilities – the most intense since the UN-sponsored ceasefire of April 2022 put an end to major military exchanges – now seems unlikely in what is seen as an attempt by the Houthis to open a second front in the Iran-US war, alongside the battle for control of Hormuz. Baraa Shiban, the Royal United Services Institute’s (Rusi) Yemen specialist, a London-based security thinktank, said the situation in the country was spiralling out of control, adding that the UN-recognised Yemeni government was opening new fronts against the Houthis in the hope of putting more pressure on their forces than they could withstand. But in the past 48 hours the Houthis had major advances south, down Yemen’s west coast, taking them closer to the high ground overlooking the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait. The fighting has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia, which on Thursday launched as many as 40 airstrikes on Houthi targets, will activate the Mecca defence agreement and ask its co-signatories, Pakistan and Turkey, to send forces. The pact is designed to be defensive in nature and believed unlikely to apply to Saudi military activities in Yemen. By taking control of more of the Red Sea coast south of the port of Hodeidah, the Houthis’ aim is to use a new lever to put pressure on Saudi Arabia and the US to agree a deal that lifts the US blockade on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf. Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged he did not expect the war with Iran to end before the US midterm elections at the start of November. The latest phase in the escalation began when Houthis attacked energy installations and southern cities in Saudi Arabia using drones and ballistic missiles. In response, the kingdom’s military forces launched at least 15 strikes between 3 and 7 September. The conflict data monitor Acled estimated there were 276 fatalities over the five-day period alone. The fighting has continued, with the Houthis claiming control of Mocha in Taiz province, as well as the inland city of Hays and the Khalid ibn al-Walid camp, the largest military base in the region. One Houthi-linked estimate suggested its forces had gained control of more than 2,320 sq miles (6,000 sq km) of land. The commander of the Yemeni government forces, Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, admitted he had organised a strategic retreat south of Mocha in order to regroup in a secure location. “The armed forces in the western coast paid a heavy price – martyrs and wounded – over the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack planned by Iran, and supported by it,” he said. Analysts claimed that the effectiveness of Yemen’s government forces was weakened by internal divisions, as well as external pressure from Saudi Arabia. The latter, meanwhile, continues to take advantage of its air superiority to attack Houthi positions, though government sources acknowledged Houthi ground advances along the coast and their missile strikes on the strategic Red Sea islands of Zuqar and Hanish. The clashes have raged across Yemen, including Ad Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwah, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, and Taiz. In the initial days of the renewed conflict the Houthis were forced back in some areas as battles on multiple fronts overstretched their resources and fighter numbers. The Houthis will be hoping political divisions inside the Yemeni government, reflected in a lack of an integrated military, will slowly give them the upper hand. The United Arab Emirates, previously a powerful player in southern Yemen where it backed the separatist forces of the Southern Transitional Council, withdrew its financial and military support at the turn of the year. The southern forces have refused to fight outside their own region. “A reduction in hostilities anytime soon seems unlikely, as both sides continue to escalate with the goal of inflicting enough damage to the other side to force a compromise,” said Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst for Acled. “In terms of military capability, both sides are more equal compared to the immediate period prior to the 2022 ceasefire when the Houthis had the upper hand.” He added: “Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in Hodeidah and Taiz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-Yemen government have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab al-Mandab.” The head of the Houthis’ national delegating negotiating team, Muhammad Abdul Salam, insisted non-Saudi commercial shipping would not be attacked. The fighting has contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80. The escalation to this week’s all-out violence has been a slow process. It began after a senior delegation of the Houthi group, which has long been in a complex alliance with Iran, flew to Tehran for the funeral of the Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in July, returning in an Iranian plane that the Saudis refused to land in rebel-controlled Sana’a. The Saudis instead bombed the runway, leading the Houthis to announce a Red Sea naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in what the Yemeni group described as a blockade for a blockade. The 20 July announcement of the blockade was followed by a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on 25 July and on a tanker off Yanbu on 24 August. Saudi Arabia has become reliant on the Red Sea route for trade after Iran throttled shipping through the strait of Hormuz as a result of US-Israeli attacks.

webTitle: Trump makes highly unusual promise of $5,000 for all if Republicans win midterms | First Thing

fields.headline: First Thing: Trump makes highly unusual promise of $5,000 for all if Republicans win midterms
fields.trailText: Speaking in Dallas, the president raised ethical concerns with an apparent $1tn offer to the electorate
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Donald Trump has pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections. The outlandish proposal, which would cost over $1tn, immediately raised ethical concerns. Trump made the promise during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in which he assailed Democrats as “radical”, defended his unpopular war in Iran, and urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot”. Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”. In a statement, Ken Martin, the chair of the Democratic National Committee, accused Republicans of holding a “bizarre dog-and-pony show” to placate the president’s “fragile ego”. “Tonight only confirmed that the president is a lame duck failure who is dragging his party toward defeat,” Martin said. Why did the Republicans hold a midterm convention? Republicans are gambling that the GOP’s first midterm convention can salvage their threatened House majority. However, Trump’s dismal approval rating drove many competitive candidates to skip the two-day event entirely. What has Trump said about the former attorney Michael Cohen? The US president has said he would consider pardoning Michael Cohen, the former fixer whom he once branded a “rat” for testifying against him. Cohen was Trump’s personal lawyer, but flipped in 2018, and pleaded guilty to federal crimes including facilitating a hush payment to the pornography star Stormy Daniels and lying under oath to Congress. Rubio says US will work with allies to stop drug-trafficking as three killed in latest boat strike The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the Trump administration was focused on working with allied countries and aligning with their laws but insisted the military would “still blow up ships if need be”. The statement comes a year after Washington began a campaign of unilateral deadly strikes against those it calls “narco-terrorists” operating boats in international waters. “I think it’s an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters,” Rubio told reporters on a trip to the Ecuadorian capital, Quito. “The important point is that these routes are being disrupted. These routes are being ended”. How many people has the US killed in its campaign? Late Wednesday, US Southern Command announced the latest strike in the Caribbean Sea, saying it killed three people. That brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the US military to at least 230 in 69 strikes. What has the US announced about Ecuador’s gangs? The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang as a terrorist organisation. Rubio said the gang was linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists. “We are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said. Apple unveils folding iPhone Duo … and its new CEO Apple has unveiled the iPhone Duo, the company’s first foldable phone and the most significant change to the iPhone since its 2007 introduction. The nearly $2,000 device takes inspiration from iPads’ wide screens, and when opened, is the company’s largest phone display and thinnest phone. While competitors have been releasing foldable smartphones since the late 2010s, the new model is a first for Apple, and its rollout serves as the first big test for its new CEO, John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook last week. The phone will be available on 23 October. What did new CEO Ternus say about his role? Helming the company’s annual showcase for the first time, Ternus said: “I want to take a moment to express what an extraordinary privilege it is to represent the remarkable teams here at Apple. I continue to be inspired every single day by the curiosity, invention and relentless pursuit of excellence that define Apple.” Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030 Artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, according to three researchers with the industry giant Anthropic, one of whom has quit his job in protest. Jacob Coxon accused Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, of ignoring or, at best, mishandling their response to the threat. He said: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. No other human activity poses this level of danger.” Lawmakers including Ted Cruz and Bernie Sanders have raised concerns following Coxon’s words. Hawaii’s western islands saw significant damage as Hurricane Lowell passed by leaving widespread power outages on Kauai. The ultrarunner Megan Eckert has shattered both the US men’s and women’s records by running 636 miles in six days. Stat of the day: Tens of millions of people fail to get humanitarian aid as global system crumbles With aid contributions cut by 30% between 2022 and 2025, the humanitarian system has suffered one of its biggest contractions since being formed in the post-second world war era, according to the State of the Humanitarian System 2026 report. webTitle: As the midterms loom, Trump returns to his happy place: on stage in the theatre of the absurd

fields.headline: As the midterms loom, Trump returns to his happy place: on stage in the theatre of the absurd
fields.trailText: President’s quest in self-mythology stops off in Dallas for a Republican convention where fans indulged his lies and revelled in his jokes
fields.bodyText: Kim Il-sung of North Korea reportedly sought transfusions of blood from young men; Mao Zedong of China believed sex with young women could prolong his life; Muammar Gaddafi underwent fat injections and hair transplantation to make himself look younger. But for Donald Trump, the secret of eternal youth lies in nights like this. The occasion of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas was enough to get the 80-year-old US president’s juices flowing. An arena with thousands of fanatical supporters indulging his lies, laughing at his jokes and burnishing his fantasies of greatness is Trump’s happy place. It certainly beats stuffy Washington. “State of the Union, you have to be very staid,” he said, feigning stiffness and a dreary voice: “Ladies and gentlemen, it’s an honour to be your president.” The crowd laughed. Trump continued: “You do that for about an hour and then everybody’s falling asleep. This is a much harder routine, let me tell you. We’re also out here to have a little bit of fun.” The crowd roared. Trump’s second term has been a quest in self-mythology. It is there in the dramatic foreign policy aimed at reshaping the world. It is there in the monuments and renovations in the capital, Washington DC. It is there in the barrage of social media posts and AI slop in which Trump appears as a young and virile all-conquering hero. It was also there on Wednesday night as Trump milked the adulation of his fanbase, the Make America Great Again diehards who, in some cases, have followed him for more than a decade. He was visibly gratified to see the “front row Joes” from his rallies, including Blake Marnell, who wears a brick-patterned suit resembling his brick wall. The president spoke for an hour and 44 minutes, surpassing his own record length convention speech set in Milwaukee two years ago. He never stopped to sip water, though the adrenaline shot of this crowd, as devoted as his aide Natalie Harp, likely could have kept him going much longer. Anyone who suspected that this unconventional convention would be a “Trump-a-palooza” had the view reinforced when Lee Greenwood sang (somewhat shakily) “God Bless the USA”, the familiar intro to Trump campaign rallies. A giant video screen with the US flag slowly rose to reveal dozens of mainly female Trump fans, waving little flags and smiling exuberantly. Trump, wearing a navy blue suit, white shirt and blue tie, walked slowly across the shiny black stage, trimmed with gold. Chants of “USA! USA!” erupted as the song finished. “Welcome to the first ever midterm convention of any party,” Trump said, conveniently ignoring three that the Democrats held in the 1970s and 1980s. He soon told another lie. “Not only is this packed, but you have an equal number of people standing outside. If anybody would like to give up their seat!” In fact there were dozens of empty seats in the stadium, with the “nosebleeds” in the upper tier mostly unfilled. Making the dubious boast that no one had left the arena after 80 minutes, the president said: “It’s a great tribute to Trump … Everybody loves me and I love everybody!” But the most grievous lie came when he falsely claimed to have won three presidential elections, and declared, also falsely, that “people on the other side are actually admitting it”. The crowd cheered and shouted: “Four more years!” This was political theatre of the absurd with many bizarre Trumpian riffs, ranging from bad sporting trades involving the Dallas Mavericks and Babe Ruth to how Trump had to sacrifice hygiene for his political career so he could shake hands (“I’m a very clean person”). In trying to champion Texas attorney general Ken Paxton for the US Senate, he said: “He may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly and he may not be the best looking guy I’ve ever seen but you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America and he deserves to be your next senator. I’m sorry, Ken. Where the hell is he? He’ll never speak to me again but that’s OK.” There were language games. He spoke as if his big idea of changing “Democrats” to “Dumocrats” was a piece of marketing genius or political artistry worthy of Lee Atwater. (“Nobody knows that dumb has a B at the end of it – most people think it’s ‘D-U-M’”.) Most reasonable people would look at him and think this poor elderly person is in need of an intervention. But this audience, of course, lapped it up and encouraged him. So he revelled in his name changes. He mentioned the “Gulf of America” and earned cheers and chants of “USA! USA!” He said, “Lake Ontario, you know we’re going to call that Lake America” – more cheers. “We did come up with one the other day which we think is appropriate. You have a neighbouring state, New Mexico. We think it should be called ‘New America.’” Turning to the Iran war and strait of Hormuz, he said: “Ladies and gentlemen, I’ll have an announcement, we’ll call it the ‘Trump Strait’ and I’m sure the Iranian leadership will be thrilled with that.” Speaking of Iran, the war would be seen as a liability by any normal president in an election year and it is a subject many Republicans would rather avoid. But Trump, true to form, bulldozed straight ahead. He also advised Iran “not to get cute” and asked the crowd: “Does anybody here think that Iran should have a nuclear weapon?” There was a huge shout of, “No!” Trump even speculated what would have happened if Iran obtained a nuclear weapon and subjugated the US. “If they had a nuclear weapon, I’d be calling the Supreme Leader and I’d be saying, ‘Mr Supreme Leader, how are you, sir? Is there anything we can do for you?’ – as opposed to bombing the crap out of him.” Somewhere in all this mess, Trump talked about the midterms. He asked voters to “pretend” that he is on the ballot and promised $5,000 to every adult US citizen if Republicans retain control of both the House and Senate. It was the old Trumpian trick: flaunt your bribery in public so blatantly that enough people assume it can’t be corrupt. He railed against Democratic “communists” and declared: “They have more bullshit than any human beings on the planet.” His supporters went wild. Such a witty putdown, sir! Trump castigated James Talarico, the Democrats’ candidate for the Senate in Texas, as “Talafreako” and claimed: “He ran a campaign to ‘beat meat.’ He called it ‘beat meat.’ I don’t know what the hell he meant by that … he wants to ‘beat meat?” … I’m getting myself in trouble. He was recently seen having a barbecue and eating a lot of meat.” All this and so much more. It went on and on, looping back on itself, zigzagging across the map, bamboozling any outside observer but somehow here, in the arena of Maga, making a warped kind of sense. “I love the weave,” Trump mused, gesticulating wildly. “You know what the weave is? You talk about something, then you bring in a ballroom, or you bring in an aeroplane, or you bring in Air Force One – but you notice I always get right back to the same topic. Some day there’ll be a time when I do the weave, weave, weave; some day there’ll be a time when I don’t get back to the original subject.” Pointing his finger in the air, Trump said: “And then you can say: he’s had it.”

webTitle: Thursday briefing: 68 facts about the Bayeux tapestry as it goes on display

fields.headline: Thursday briefing: 68 facts about the Bayeux tapestry as it goes on display
fields.trailText: In today’s newsletter: No Bayeux ticket? Everything you need to know about the sold-out exhibition – from its epic journey to London to a Game of Thrones likeness
fields.bodyText: Good morning. If you live in the UK, you have probably heard about the Bayeux tapestry exhibition, which opens today, and you probably haven’t got a ticket. The digital queue was nine-hours long when they first went on sale in July, and the exhibition has already broken the British Museum’s record for the number of tickets sold in a single day. Some lucky individuals, including King Charles and aspiring overlord Peter Thiel, have been treated to early previews of the medieval tapestry. Guests staying at One Aldwych, a hotel where rooms go for £1,000 a night, can partake in the “Bayeux experience” with a themed cocktail (mead spritzer, anyone?), a full English breakfast and preferential access to tickets. In a break from our regular programming, this morning’s newsletter brings you 68 facts about the Bayeux tapestry for anyone who hasn’t been able to see the real thing. That’s one fact for each of its 68 metres (bonus fact: it’s 68.3m long). If that’s not your vibe, just be glad I didn’t manage to find 1066 facts. First, here are the headlines. Five big stories Reform | The Met police will investigate allegations that Reform UK broke electoral law relating to overseas donations as part of a wider inquiry. UK- Israel | Prominent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end. Technology | Just a day after three Anthropic researchers warned that artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, US politicians have begun lashing out about the risks of the burgeoning technology. UK news | Protesters who gathered outside a Portsmouth hotel mistook Pakistan’s under-19 cricket team for asylum seekers. US news | Donald Trump pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections, during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas. In depth: From nudity, a save from the Nazis and its restoration, a buffet of Bayeux facts 1. First of all, as the exhibition’s curator Michael Lewis points out in his book, the Bayeux tapestry isn’t really a tapestry. It’s “more accurately described as an embroidery”, Lewis writes. (Nobody actually calls it an embroidery, though, so we’ll stick with tapestry). 2. The embroidery tapestry tells the story of the events that culminated in the Battle of Hastings in 1066, when William the Conquerer defeated King Harold. 3. It was supposedly commissioned by Bishop Odo, William the Conquerer’s half-brother, for his newly built cathedral in Bayeux in 1077. He was prone to “self-aggrandisement” (in Lewis’s words), which is why he gave himself a starring role in the tapestry. 4. But it wasn’t made in Bayeux. Researchers think it was probably made in England, near Canterbury. 5. It’s embroidered on linen, with 10 colours of woollen thread likely dyed with woad, madder and indigo. 6. Its nine panels were embroidered separately, and then stitched together to form a continuous picture. 7. It features 623 men, 190 horses, 35 dogs, 37 buildings (including Mont-Saint-Michel) and 41 ships. 8. It may have had a single master designer who plotted its narrative, but … 9. The embroidery was almost certainly stitched by multiple women (William of Poitiers cited English women as skilled embroiderers). 10. It’s unclear how long it took them – one estimate reckons the stitching took between two and four years. 11. Yet, only three women actually feature in the tapestry. None of them are having a good time: one is weeping at her husband’s deathbed, another is fleeing a burning building and a third is being assaulted by a priest. 12. This third figure is Ælfgyva (meaning elf-gift), the only named woman in the tapestry. Scholars think that she could be Emma of Normandy, who was accused of having an affair with the Bishop of Winchester. 13. The tapestry conveniently doesn’t mention Edgar Ætheling, who had a stronger hereditary claim to the English throne in 1066 than either William or Harold. 14. The borders tell their own stories. They’re filled with fantastical beasts, creating what the Guardian’s art critic Jonathan Jones described as a “marginal world of monsters and myths”. 15. The upper border features one of the first depictions of Haley’s Comet. 16. The tapestry also shows a figure with the name Harold, depicting the famous (and probably apocryphal) moment he was struck in the eye by an arrow. Most scholars think Harold was actually hacked to death. 17. It was possibly designed to be interpreted by a live storyteller in front of an audience, much like an epic poem. 18. It’s damaged at the end, and incomplete. Nobody knows what scene would have finished the tapestry (some think it could have been a depiction of William’s coronation at Westminster Abbey in 1066). 19. It survived at least three fires in Bayeux Cathedral. 20. The first recorded reference to the tapestry was in the 1476 inventory of Bayeux cathedral, which described a “very long and narrow hanging of linen, embroidered with figures and inscriptions representing the Conquest of England.” 21. The tapestry hasn’t always been well looked after. For centuries it was rolled out for cathedral visitors. One visiting English antiquary observed in the early 1800s that it was “much rubbed at the beginning, torn towards the end.” 22. In 1792, during the French Revolution, the tapestry was nearly used to cover a wagon (it was saved at the last minute by an official who swapped it for a piece of canvas). 23. In 1794, an proposal was briefly floated to cut the tapestry into strips to decorate a festival float. 24. A 19th-century British artist secretly snipped off two fragments that ended up in a London museum (these were eventually returned to Bayeux). 25. In 1803, Napoleon had the tapestry temporarily moved from Bayeux to Paris, where it hung on display at the Louvre, to rally support for his planned invasion of Britain. 26. The first full photographic copy of the tapestry was made for the South Kensington Museum in 1872 (now the V&A museum). 27. A group of women in Staffordshire created the largest Bayeux reproduction in 1885, which is displayed in Reading Museum. It took them 18 months. 28. They removed 93 penises from their reproduction, 88 belonging to horses and five to men. 29. The Nazis saw the tapestry as a propaganda tool, and wanted to establish that Normans were actually the descendants of Viking settlers. 30. They appointed a professor of Viking archaeology as the leader of “Special Assignment Bayeaux” to study it. 31. Heinrich Himmler tasked two SS officers in 1944 to seize the Bayeaux tapestry from the basement of the Louvre, where it was being stored. 32. A group of local resistance fighters tipped off by code breakers at Bletchley Park managed to intercept the officers and protect the tapestry. 33. Since 1983, the tapestry has been displayed at the Bayeux museum, in a 17th-century seminary near Bayeux’s medieval town centre. 34. When the tapestry arrived at the Bayeux museum in the 1980s, photos show that it appeared to have been folded and hoisted up a stairwell. 35. It’s incredibly fragile, and liable to fray. A 2020 study found the tapestry had “24,204 stains, 16,445 wrinkles, 9,646 gaps in the cloth or the embroidery” and “30 non-stabilised tears.” 36. The first request for the Bayeux tapestry to be loaned to Britain was in 1953, for Queen Elizabeth II’s coronation. The French refused. 37. Another request was made in 1966, to mark the 900th anniversary of the Battle of Hastings. The French refused, again. 38. In 2013, a committee was formed to advise on how the tapestry could be redisplayed. It raised the prospect of a loan to the UK (“I did sort of bang on about it,” Lewis, a committee member, later recalled, “until I was a bit like a broken record”). 39. The Bayeux museum was scheduled to be closed for refurbishment, creating an opportunity for the tapestry to travel on loan. 40. In January 2018, Emmanuel Macron announced at a summit with Theresa May that the French had agreed to loan the tapestry. Although France had “found the best experts of the world to explain in perfect detail” why the loan “was impossible”, Macron said that the French government had “decided” otherwise. 41. Many people insist it should never have been moved. Arts journalist Didier Rykner started a petition against the loan that gained more than 70,000 signatures. 42. The late David Hockney agreed, described the loan as “madness,” and said “some things are too precious to take a risk with.” 43. And two expert reports in 2021 and 2022 advised Macron against the transportation of the tapestry. 44. The loan specified the tapestry had to be stored lying flat, and couldn’t be subject to tremors any greater than two millimetres per second during its transportation. 45. A team of conservators and experts, including a German vibration technology scientist, were involved with its relocation. They designed a meticulous solution for transporting the tapestry involving a “paravent”, a hinged folding screen on wheels. 46. The paravent was designed so it could be closed into a rectangular block with the tapestry inside, effectively folded 28 times. 47. It took ninety people in blue latex gloves seven hours working to extract the tapestry from its case and transfer it to the paravent. 48. It then had to be stored in a specially manufactured crate for shipping. The art logistics firm Hizikia built two nesting crates, with an outer aluminium crate designed to reduce the impact of movement. 49. The firm also provided a customised reinforced truck to dampen vibrations. 50. Experts carried out two dry runs, one with a replica tapestry transported across the channel that made its way to an art warehouse in south London. 51. Data from these dry-runs showed that French roads are smoother than British roads. 52. The tapestry has been insured by the Treasury’s indemnity scheme for £800m, which is more than twice the value of the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction (Salvator Mundi, a painting of Jesus attributed to Leonardo da Vinci). 53. Two threads were reportedly broken when the tapestry arrived in London. 54. At the British Museum, it will be housed in a custom-made case, believed to be the longest ever constructed, and will be exposed to a limited number of light hours per day. 55. When the lights are switched on, they’ll be dimmed to 50 lux, the international museum standard for sensitive materials. 56. Andy Burnham, Emmanuel Macron and King Charles viewed the tapestry last Wednesday. 57. It will be displayed at the British Museum until July 2027, before it returns to a newly built museum in Normandy that will open later next year. 58. Nicholas Cullinan, director of the British Museum, has said he hopes the Bayeux loan could revive the prospect for a loan of the Parthenon marbles. 59. The tapestry has inspired numerous copycats, including the Bloody Sunday Tapestry created by the artist Darren Cullen in 2013. 60. There’s also a Game of Thrones Tapestry at the Ulster Museum in Belfast. 61. The Sun newspaper commissioned a “Bye-EU” tapestry in 2018 to commemorate the Brexit vote, which depicted Boris Johnson in chain mail and Theresa May surrounded by the decapitated corpses of Brussels bureaucrats. 62. A helmet from Sutton Hoo, and the Lewis chess pieces, were both loaned to Normandy museums as part of the Bayeux loan. 63. My favourite bit of any trip to the British Museum is the gift shop (eds: does this count as a fact?), where you can now buy a replica Norman helmet and bottle of Bayeux mead with your Tutankhamun pencil tin. 64. Speaking of Bayeux tat, Nigel Farage sported a Bayeux-themed tie during the 2014 Rochester byelection, a reminder of “the last time we were invaded and taken over”. 65. Radio 4 has devoted a special day of broadcasts to mark the arrival of the tapestry. 66. And the museum’s videos about the tapestry’s arrival are narrated by the Traitors presenter Claudia Winkleman. 67. Philippe Bélavel, Macron’s former culture adviser, has said “such a loan will only happen once and never again.” 68. The next wave of public tickets for the tapestry, which cost £33, will go on sale on 21 October at 10am. Best of luck getting yours. What else we’ve been enjoying I loved Micha Frazer-Carroll’s brilliant newsletter exploring how and why generations of Black athletes have become style icons. Sign up to receive the Long Wave in your inbox here. Michael Segalov, newsletters team J Oliver Conroy’s long piece on what happened to Turning Point USA in the year after the killing of Charlie Kirk is a compelling, frightening read on the future of the American right. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team Among all the tributes, I found these reflections on Gloria Steinem’s legacy from a host of contemporary feminist writers to be a particularly powerful homage. Michael Resident sex expert Alix Fox hosted this riveting reader Q&A yesterday, fielding your queries on making time for intimacy in parenthood, the rise of audio erotica, and why trendy sex toys are apparently shaped like fruit now. Charlie I watched the trailer for Andrew Garfield’s new film The Uprising while at the cinema last weekend (the Odyssey; quite long?), and Peter Bradhsaw’s cutting review confirmed my initial instinct to steer well clear. Tennis | Elena Rybakina will become the No 1 woman in the world for the first time after orchestrating a supreme recovery to reach the semi-finals of the US Open with a 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 win over the Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen. Cycling | Matthew Brennan claimed a fifth stage victory on Wednesday as the young British rider edged a bunch sprint in Seville to win the 17th stage. The Times says “Farage faces Met inquiry over Reform donations”, the i Paper also has “Police set to interview Farage over Reform UK donations”, and the Mirror writes “Farage faces cop quiz on donors”. The FT has “US spy chief to take stronger role in stalled Ukraine talks”, the Mail writes “Burnham: National security can’t come at the expense of social security”, and the Express leads with “The King has spoken with Harry since return”. The Telegraph splashes “Labour’s new tax assault on hospitality”, and on air traffic chaos, Metro has “Ready for departure?” Today in Focus: The Latest Why is Trump silent on UK sanctions against Israeli West Bank settlements?
