webTitle: US citizens will receive $5,000 if Republicans win midterms, Trump claims in lengthy convention speech

fields.headline: US citizens will receive $5,000 if Republicans win midterms, Trump claims in lengthy convention speech
fields.trailText: President makes offer that would cost US over $1tn and asks voters to ‘pretend that I’m on the ballot’ despite being deeply unpopular among electorate
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections, during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in which the president assailed Democrats as “radical” and defended his unpopular war in Iran. The outlandish proposal, which would cost over $1tn, immediately raised ethical concerns. But it laid bare the extent of the Republicans’ concern about their prospects in the pivotal November elections. “If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump told a roaring crowd, during a nearly two-hour speech in which he also urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot” – despite his historic unpopularity causing many vulnerable Republican politicians to avoid the event. Surrounded by supporters waving American flag placards, Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”, but devoted much of his speech to fearmongering about what would happen should Democrats win the House or the Senate for the final two years of his presidency. “There is a crazy little sick cloud over our country,” Trump said. “We will defeat communism in America.” The president and Republicans are gambling that throwing a midterm convention – the first the GOP has ever held – can buoy the party, which is predicted to lose control of the House. Yet, Trump’s deep unpopularity among Americans – his approval rating is hovering at about 38% – meant many Republican candidates running in competitive races skipped the two-day confab entirely. Even so, Trump’s speech made it clear he thinks he will be the deciding factor in November. Noting that the party which holds the White House traditionally struggles in the midterm elections, Trump said: “We’ve got to change that, because we have something going that’s so good. “If we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security, you’re going to lose your wealth. Our country is going through hell – we will be going through hell, just like we did, just two years ago,” he said. The buildup to the midterm convention had somewhat of a chaotic air. Trump was initially scheduled to speak on the second night, before the Republican National Committee announced that he would deliver the keynote on Wednesday, and instead give closing remarks on Thursday after his vice-president, JD Vance, speaks. Trump made several references to the war in Iran, warning Tehran “not to get cute” or the US “will have to hit them very hard”. But he also appeared to acknowledge the economic pain caused by the soaring price of oil. Trump re-enacted the way he told his economic advisers that the US needed to start the conflict because Iran was “two, maybe three weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”. “I hate to do this to you,” he said he told them, noting the economy had been doing well. At the convention center, there were signs of middling enthusiasm among the rank and file. Compared with the four-day traditional convention in Milwaukee two years ago, the first day felt muted. There were no long queues to enter, no eternal waits for food or bathrooms. Swathes of empty seats were visible throughout Trump’s speech. Visible, except to Trump, who claimed, wrongly, that the arena was full. “Not only is this packed but you have an equal number of people standing outside,” Trump declared. This was not observed by Guardian reporters. The RNC had announced in mid-August that Americans could apply for tickets to attend the event, suggesting that applicants would enter a lottery and only a lucky few would be granted access. Yet on Wednesday, with the convention under way, applications for tickets were instantly being granted on an RNC sign-up page. Trump himself, however, appeared energized in his call to action on the first night, cracking jokes, including at the expense of Ken Paxton, his handpicked candidate for Senate in Texas who won a primary against the incumbent John Cornyn earlier this year. “He may not dress right. He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Trump said of Paxton. “But you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America.” Trump spent several minutes attacking Democrats, including Paxton’s opponent, James Talarico, who Trump mocked as a “weird-looking dude”; the former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper, who is now running for Senate; and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan. In a statement, Ken Martin, the chair of the Democratic National Committee, accused Republicans of holding a “bizarre dog-and-pony show” to placate the president’s “fragile ego”. “Tonight only confirmed that the president is a lame duck failure who is dragging his party toward defeat,” Martin said. The Republicans’ unusual midterm convention features 12 hours of programming across two nights. On Wednesday, the speaker lineup featured Trump loyalists and candidates, but showmanship remained at the center of the agenda. Byron Donalds, a rising star in the party who is running for governor of Florida, and Mehmet Oz and Scott Bessent, two of Trump’s cabinet secretaries, were among those to take the stage, yet the president, a UFC fan, decided he would be introduced by two fighters, the middleweight Bo Nickal and Justin “The Highlight” Gaethje, a lightweight. Most speakers only got five minutes. Nickal and Gaethje, who both fought at the UFC 250 event on the White House Lawn in June, got 10. Gaethje told the crowd he had earned his “Highlight” nickname when he knocked out his first opponent very quickly in 2016, before linking himself to the 80-year-old Trump. “One mistake I’ve made in my career was becoming complacent while I was on a winning streak and forgetting how unforgiving my sport would be,” Gaethje said. “If we are not just as passionate about voting and winning in these midterms as we were in the last presidential election, then we risk being knocked out and losing all the momentum we have been fighting for.” Earlier, Republicans said the focus would be on “lowering costs, securing our border, making our communities safer, and putting American workers and families first”. Yet speaker after speaker instead attacked Democrats on alleged support for transgender rights, in particular, suggesting the Republican party intends to put culture wars towards the front as November approaches. Trump will speak again on Thursday, but said his address would be much briefer. “I gave you a lot of material,” he said, capping his remarks on Wednesday, before pleading one more time with voters to “please pretend that I’m running”. • This article was amended on 10 September 2026. An earlier version incorrectly described Roy Cooper as a Republican.

fields.headline: Trump claims he will give $5,000 to every American if Republicans win the midterms as he defends Iran war and tariffs– as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: In a nearly two-hour speech, Donald Trump capped off his first night remarks at the GOP midterm convention by pleading with Republicans to “pretend that I’m running”. The president centered himself in the battle to control Congress, and acknowledged that candidates are more successful when he is on the ballot. He offered an ominous outlook if Republicans fail to retain power. “If we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security. You’re going to lose your wealth. Our country is going through hell. You will be going through hell just like you did just two years ago,” Trump said. The president made the stunning claim that he would send every citizen $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the US House and Senate. However, he provided no details about where he would source this money from or the legality of the incentive. “It will be called the Trump dividend,” the president said. A reminder that it’s against federal law to “make or offer to make an expenditure to any person, either to vote or withhold his vote”. It would cost over $1tn, accounting for more than 235 million adult citizens across the country. Throughout his remarks, Trump also tried to campaign on behalf on Republicans in competitive midterm races. While he made fun of Ken Paxton’s clothing choices and the way he speaks, he praised the Republican nominee for US Senate in Texas as “the single greatest attorney general” in the state’s history, while also branding his opponent James Talarico as a “disaster”. He also praised Michael Whatley, who is running to keep the open Senate seat in North Carolina red, and blasted his challenger – the state’s former Democratic governor Roy Cooper – over his handling of the devastating hurricane that swept through the state in 2024. Earlier, Democratic senator John Fetterman made a surprise virtual appearance at the Republican midterm convention, delivering a video address supporting Dave McCormick, a Republican senator in Pennsylvania. Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with his party since his election in 2022, said in the video that he would always reject “extremes and socialism”, repeating an oft-used Republican critique of the Democratic party’s increasingly popular left wing. “Yes, I’m a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today? Because well, I’m a commonsense Democrat. I’m always going to stand with America,” the Pennsylvania lawmaker said in the pre-recorded message. Fetterman, for his part, insisted that he would not be switching parties in the next Congress. ““I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party-and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on,” he said in a statement. Meanwhile, several Republicans who are facing tough races have chosen not to attend the convention in Dallas. This include Susan Collins, the five-term incumbent senator from Maine, and Dan Sullivan – the Republican senator from Alaska who is facing a tough contest against former Democratic congresswoman Mary Peltola. By showing up at the convention, these nominees run the risk of isolating swing voters they need to court in competitive districts and states where the administration’s policies have proven unpopular. In a nearly two-hour speech, Donald Trump capped off his first night remarks at the GOP midterm convention by repeating his plea to Republicans. “Please pretend that I’m running,” he said. “Get out and vote on November 3rd or sooner, because in actuality, I really am running … we have to take Congress.” The president noted that he’ll also speak on the second and final night of the convention, but it won’t be as long. “I’m not doing a big deal like this because I don’t have to say the same stuff twice. I gave you a lot of material,” he said. “I’m going to be just sort of getting up here and saying, good luck. We love you all.” Also in his speech, Trump referenced the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk – which happened a year ago on Thursday. Erika, Kirk’s widow who is now leading his organization, Turning Point USA, was in the audience. Those at the American Airlines Center gave Erika a standing ovation, while Trump chided people who “cheered” Kirk’s death. “The mask came off the radical left,” the president said. As we’ve previously reported, by November of 2025, a Reuters investigation estimated that 600 people had been terminated, disciplined, investigated, suspended or otherwise admonished for their Kirk posts, likening the reaction to an ideological purge. The so-called “Trump dividend” would cost more than $1tn – accounting for more than 235 million US adult citizens. The president has given shout outs to several Republicans running for Senate in a number of competitive races throughout his speech. He boosted Michael Whatley – the former RNC chair who is the GOP nominee for Senate in North Carolina. Whatley is facing Roy Cooper – the state’s former governor – as they vie for the open seat that the incumbent senator, Thom Tillis, is vacating. Trump took aim at Cooper’s handling of the aftermath of Hurricane Helene – the devastating storm that killed at least 107 people and caused nearly $60bn in damage. “[Cooper] did nothing to help. He was a disaster during that very traumatic time,” the president said. However, as my colleague Chris Stein has reported, when Trump visited the state shortly after returning to office, he said Whatley would be “in charge of making sure everything goes well” with the recovery. That’s led to Whatley being known in the state’s press as the “recovery czar”, a title the Republican’s campaign said he was never given, but which Cooper has wielded to argue that his opponent is the one letting North Carolinians down. Trump defended the war in Iran during his speech today, and appeared to downplay concerns about the price of gas – now more than a dollar higher per gallon than this time last year. “Let me ask you one question: Can Iran have a nuclear weapon? Absolutely not,” he said. The economic ramifications of the conflict, including record-high inflation, have had an impact on voters. Poll after poll shows a majority of Americans disapprove of Trump’s decision to go to war. Earlier, the president spoke about his prized White House ballroom. The supreme court recently allowed construction to continue after several legal challenges. Again, Trump claimed that this is a “tax free” project. “I’m giving you a ballroom free of charge,” the president insisted. But the Guardian previously reported that the administration quietly redirected $352m in federal funds designated for the Secret Service toward the ballroom project, despite repeated promises by Trump that the construction would be financed by private donations. The funds were drawn from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Trump’s signature tax legislation passed last summer on Republican-only votes. The law stipulates the money may only be spent on Secret Service personnel, training facilities, technology and related costs, not construction. A reminder that Congress explicitly refused to provide $1bn in funds for the “East Wing Modernization Project” in June. It’s unclear on what legal grounds the president can offer a cash incentive to vote for Republicans ahead of the midterm elections. It is against federal law to “make or offer to make an expenditure to any person, either to vote or withhold his vote”. Trump has claimed he will send every citizen $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the US House and Senate. He provided no details about where he would source this money from or the legality of the incentive. “So if the Republicans win, you win with us … it will be called the Trump dividend,” the president said. Trump went on to claim Democrats are opposing his sweeping legislation that requires voter ID in order to cast a ballot, as well as proof of citizenship in order to register, “because they want to cheat”. “You have to admit they’re really good at this stuff, they come up with more excuses,” the president said. Democrats and a small number of Republicans have said their concerns about the stalled bill – known as the Save America act – are that it would actually make it harder for eligible voters from casting a ballot. Trump went on to praise top House Republican Mike Johnson – who he branded as the “greatest speaker” in history, and Senate majority leader John Thune. Thune’s name, however, was met with boos. Trump came to the top senator’s defense. “John is working hard. He’s got great opposition,” the president said. As Trump continues his rechristening streak, he repeated his suggestion to rename the strait of Hormuz as the “Trump strait”, which was met with cheers across the arena. This comes after Trump signed executive orders to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” and Lake Ontario as “Lake America.” Donald Trump falsely claimed that there have been “zero” border crossings over the last 16 months. He also falsely claimed there were “25 million” under his predecessor Joe Biden. While there has been a steep drop in encounters at the southern border, there have been almost 600,000 since January 2025. Meanwhile, most estimates suggest that there were about 11 million throughout the Biden administration – less than half of the number Trump has claimed. Trump has used parts of his speech to direct Texans to vote for Ken Paxton in the US Senate race in November. The beleaguered attorney general is facing Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico in one of the most competitive contests this midterm cycle. Several recent polls show Talarico leading Paxton. A reminder that no Democrat has actually won statewide office in Texas since 1994. “Some may not like the way he dresses. I don’t. Although tonight he looked very spiffy in his blue suit, I must tell you. But they may not like the way he talks. I can see that, you know,” Trump said. “You may not like the way he looks, but here’s the news. In the history of Texas, he is the single greatest attorney general you’ve ever had, and maybe the top attorney general in the whole United States.” “When I’m on the ticket, Republicans always do very well,” Trump said, before repeating the false claim that he has “won the presidency three times”. Trump won the 2016 and 2014 presidential elections but lost the 2020 election – despite routinely falsely insisting that the election was “rigged” and “stolen”. Trump repeated that there are about “35 races” which are competitive this midterm cycle. However, a number of vulnerable Republicans have to be careful about yolking themselves to the administration – particularly in districts and states who disapprove of the president’s policies. Trump added that he’ll spend time over the next two months campaigning on behalf of the candidates in key battlegrounds. “I’m going to go to every one of those states for congressmen and for senators. I’m going to do that, and we’re going to have rallies,” the president said. “ The president implored attendees and voters throughout the country to “pretend that I’m on the ballot” as they cast their votes in this year’s midterms. “I’m on the ballot, just one more time,” he added. “Because if we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security. You’re going to lose your wealth. Our country is going through hell. You will be going through hell just like you did just two years ago.” Trump congratulated himself within the first few minutes of speaking. “I want you to remember me in four or five years when this country is rocketing. Remember, I’m the one that got it started,” he said. Cheers erupted and calls for him to “run in 2028” could be heard. Running for a third term is something the president frequently floats, even thought the constitution limits him to two non-consectutive terms in office. The president made his case clear in his opening remarks to attendees. “Your vote will decide whether our country stumbles at the starting gate of the next 250 years or surges forward and never ever looks back,” he said. “Hand America’s future to the radical left Democrats, and our nation will spend the next decade just getting back on its feet. It will be a tragedy. Vote Republican and we will leave the world in our dust for generations to come. There’ll be nothing like it.” Trump acknowledged that the convention was thrown together in eight weeks, and insisted that the arena is “packed”. However, as my colleagues Adam Gabbatt and David Smith report from Dallas, there are several parts of the American Airlines Center with empty seats. Donald Trump walked on stage at the American Airlines Center in Dallas with a live performance from Lee Greenwood singing God Bless the USA – Trump’s mainstay anthem that plays at all of his campaign and presidential events. “Welcome to the first ever midterm convention of any party,” the president said. “Took a little imagination to think of it, but we thought of it.” We’re seeing backlash trickle in from Democrats over Senator John Fetterman’s video message that played at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas. “A year ago I labeled John Fetterman ‘Trump’s favorite Democrat’. Tonight, he yet again proves why,” said Congressman Brendan Boyle, a Pennsylvania Democrat. Meanwhile Sarah McBride, the sole US representative for Delaware and the first openly transgender member of Congress, said that “being a Democratic politician who decides to speak at Trump’s midterm convention is like boarding the Titanic after it hit the iceberg”. Ahead of Donald Trump’s speech in Dallas, Justin Gaethje – an MMA fighter who took part in the UFC match at the White House in June – took the stage. “This is about supporting President Trump and sending him Republican allies in Congress to continue moving forward with his agenda for the economy, national security, and the country. So let’s get behind him,” Gaethje said. “We have seen what will happen if we give away the midterms to complacency, we cannot do that again.” Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, addressed attendees at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, where he slammed former president Joe Biden. He accused Biden and Democrats of bringing the US “to the brink of ruin”. “They opened our borders and shuttered our factories. They imposed one set of rules on American workers, while allowing our competitors to play by another, inflation soared to a 40-year high,” Bessent said. This, despite the fact that current prices are actually higher than when Biden left office in 2025, according to the latest inflation date. “This summer, we celebrated what our founders began. This fall, we will decide faithfully how we preserve it,” Bessent added. “We’ve come a long way under President Trump. Now it falls on us to show up when it matters the most to continue this fight.” Here are a few more pictures from the GOP midterm convention Reporting from Dallas Mike Lawler, the vulnerable Republican congressman running for reelection in New York, has defended his decision to attend the midterm convention. As we reported earlier, numerous Republicans running in swing districts have stayed away from the event, wary of being associated with Trump, but Lawler is among those due to speak here on Wednesday. Speaking to reporters outside the convention hall, Lawler was why he decided to appear at the Trump-heavy event, when others have stayed away. “Well, he’s the president of the United States, and whether people want to say yay or nay, the fact is he’s the president. Two, this is an opportunity to talk about what we’ve actually done, and my speech is going to focus on what I’ve delivered for my district, and in fact, standing up to the president to do it,” Lawler said. Lawler represents New York’s 17th district, which Kamala Harris won, narrowly, in 2024, and the Cook report rates the race as a “toss up” between Lawler and Cait Conley, his Democratic opponent. He claimed he has “loudly and vocally pushed back” against Trump on issues including funding to Ukraine, adding: “I have the ability to deal with the president, just screaming and yelling and saying ‘I hate Donald Trump’ gets you there. Nothing.” Members of Congress reportedly had to pay $25,000 to attend the convention, but Lawler said he hadn’t stumped up that amount. “I didn’t pay anything other than a plane ticket and a hotel room,” he said. Ahead of his appearance on stage, a video about Laken Riley, the University of Georgian nursing student who was murdered by an undocumented immigant in 2024, was played for the audience in Dallas. Riley’s death became a flashpoint for the hard-right to eventually introduce, and pass, legislation that mandates the detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related crimes, and allows state attorneys general to sue the federal government if they believe their states have been harmed by its failure to enforce immigration laws. Several House and Senate Democrats, including Osoff, joined Republicans to advance the bill, which Trump signed into law last year. “Every life taken by an illegal immigrant is preventable, but it can only be stopped when we have leaders that will prioritize Americans,” said Collins, who was one of the legislation’s authors. “I sat in Jon Ossoff’s office and demanded that he help America remember the name of our shared constituent, but no, he wouldn’t lift a finger to help me. He forgot her name until it was politically convenient.” A reminder that Senator John Fetterman, the Pennsylvania Democrat, has been frequently dodging work, as well as his own constituents, the Wall Street Journal reported last week. Dave McCormick is the kind of senator that gets the job done, and he’s going to fight for Pennsylvania.” In the stunning display of support for a Republican colleague in the Senate, Fetterman called McCormick his “great friend”, and said that he will work with him and Donald Trump “to fight and defend the steel way of life”. Ohio Senator John Husted, another Republican facing a tough race in November, spent time attacking his Democratic challenger, Sherrod Brown – a former senator who lost his seat in 2024. “It’s also hard to explain why Joe Biden and Sherrod Brown raised our taxes to fund benefits for illegals and shift our jobs to China,” Husted said. “Sherrod Brown put Shanghai over Steubenville and Beijing over Brunswick, didn’t he, Ohio?” One of the more vulnerable Republicans who IS at the GOP midterm convention is Representative Rob Bresnahan – a Pennsylvania Republican who flipped his seat red in 2024, but is facing a tough race this November. Ken Paxton, Texas’ attorney general and the Republican nominee for US Senate in the state, is now delivering a speech that is supposed to be focused on affordability. But Paxton spent time issuing several digs at his Democratic rival, James Talarico. “I will fight to preserve the American dream. James Talarico is running to destroy it,” Paxton said. “This guy is really obsessed with transitions. He wants to transition your kids. He wants to transition Texas off of oil and gas. How about we transition him and his crazy ideas right out of Texas?” Before he left the stage, Paxton said that if he loses the Texas Senate seat “we lose the commonsense revolution”. The scandal-plagued Republican received Trump’s endorsement, that allowed him to defeat the incumbent John Cornyn in the GOP primary earlier this year. John Fetterman – the Democratic senator from Pennsylvania who has found himself increasingly estranged from his party – is set to issue a video message praising Donald Trump at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, according to a report from Axios. The first-term lawmaker – who has cast several votes bucking Democrats – will be in the video that will play ahead of his colleague Senator Dave McCormick’s appearance on stage. McCormick helped arrange Fetterman’s appearance, according to one of Axios’ sources with knowledge of the situation. Fetterman was the sole Democrat to vote no on several war powers resolutions to curb the Trump administration’s military action in Iran. Earlier this year, he voted to confirm Trump’s pick to lead the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Markwayne Mullin, and last year Fetterman routinely joined Republicans on key votes to keep the government open – while Senate Democrats withheld support for key appopriations bills to protest expiring Affordable Care Act subsidies. According to a New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena poll in August, 74% of Democrats in Pennsylvania had a favorable opinion of Fetterman in 2024 – two years after he won his Senate election – that has now fallen to 22%. Meanwhile, only 25 % of Pennsylvania Repbublicans viewed Fetterman favorably in 2024. That number has shot up to 73%. Despite not confirming whether he would seek a second term in office, Fetterman recently said that he has no intention to switch parties. He has, however, issued a caveat – he would consider leaving the Democratic caucus if it became the “anti-Israel party”. Fetterman has emerged as one of Israel’s most prominent advocates among Senate Democrats, even as others in the party back away from their traditional support for the country amid accusations that prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government committed genocide in Gaza. Opponents of congressional redistricting in Missouri appealed to the US supreme court on Wednesday after a federal panel let stand a ruling allowing the state to use a new map backed by Donald Trump in November’s midterms. The map’s challengers, including a group ‌opposed to the Republican-drawn map called People Not Politicians, made the request in an emergency ⁠filing, moving swiftly after Stephen Clark, a St Louis-based chief US district judge, ‌issued his decision on Tuesday. Clashing rulings had plunged Missouri’s congressional elections into uncertainty, less than two months out from the crucial midterms that will decide which party controls a closely divided congress – and will impact the fate of Trump’s agenda for the rest of his term. First, the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh had denied an emergency request from Missouri officials to use a congressional map in November that was redrawn with Trump’s support to give the GOP an edge in the midterms. That decision effectively allowed a Missouri supreme court ruling to revert back to the 2022 map to stand. Not long after, a ruling by Clark, who was appointed by Trump, issued a contradictory decision, temporarily preventing the state from using its old congressional maps in the November elections. The temporary restraining order, or TRO, ordered Missouri to use the newly drawn districts that favor Republicans, which the state used in its August primary elections. Clark’s order was then swiftly appealed to the eighth US circuit court of appeals. During his remarks in Dallas, Michael Whatley – the former Republican National Committee (RNC) chair and GOP nominee for US Senate in North Carolina – avoided spending much time talking about the Trump administration’s policies like tariffs, the war in Iran and the ensuing economic strain. Instead, Whatley spent much of his speech denigrating his Democratic challenger – former governor Roy Cooper. Whatley said the “blood” of Iryna Zarutska – the Ukrainian refugee who was fatally stabbed onboard a light rail train in Charlotte by Decarlos Brown Jr – is on Cooper’s “hands”. Brown has a documented history of prior arrests, other legal problems and mental health issues. However, the Trump administration and its Republican allies seized on the case, claiming the killing demonstrated how local leaders, judges and policies in Democratic-led cities were failing to protect residents from violent crime. “That monster should have never been on the streets,” Whatley said in Dallas. “When it comes to keeping our kids and our communities safe, Roy Cooper was the worst governor in the history of North Carolina.” While there are dozens of Republican lawmakers and candidates who are facing tough races in November at the convention in Dallas over the next two days, there are several who have chosen not to attend the event that has been hastily thrown together at the behest of Donald Trump. This includes Susan Collins, the five-term incumbent senator from Maine, who is contending with a deluge of anti-Trump animus in her purple state ahead of her re-election race. Her campaign has told various outlets that she would be constituents back in Maine during the convention. Similarly, Dan Sullivan – the Republican senator from Alaska who is facing a tough contest against former Democratic congresswoman Mary Peltola – is opting to skip the event. Sullivan has spent Wednesday on the trail in Alaska, posting videos and photos from various campaign stops. This comes after the US president said last week that he would travel to the state to campaign on behalf of Sullivan ahead of the general election. Meanwhile, Tom Barrett, a Michigan representative, and Tom Tiffany, the congressman and Republican nominee for Wisconsin governor, are some of the House members – seen as vulnerable in their respective races – who will also not attend the GOP convention in Dallas. If these nominees show up in Dallas, they could run the risk of isolating swing voters they need to court. Earlier, Trump snapped at an ABC News reporter who asked about the absences. “We have room for the ones that have a close race, if they’re slightly behind or slightly ahead or tied,” the president said. “But we don’t have room for people that are 35 points up and don’t need to be there … Every politician that we’ve wanted to be there is there.” Reporting from Dallas The midterm convention is under way. Each speaker stands at a lectern on a shiny black stage with big blue star and gold trim. There are four US national flags and five giant video screens behind them. Earlier today, the screens showed dark, spooky images of Democrats Elizabeth Warren, Bernie Sanders, Kamala Harris, Joe Biden, Nancy Pelosi and Tim Walz. The red-carpeted convention floor looks full and has the familiar vertical signs with the names of individual states, even though state delegates have not been elected this time. There is also a flavour of a Donald Trump campaign rally: the so-called “Front row Joes” are here, as are the “Trump Tribe of Texas” with “Lady Liberty” (a woman dressed in a Statue of Liberty costume). Blake Marnell, wearing his customary brick patterned suit and tie and red “Make America great again” cap, told me: “There’s probably no administration in history that you can look at two years in and say we got everything we wanted but I’m overall extremely happy. My number one issue of course is the border. There are a lot of other issues that are important, but I think that most of those are downstream from illegal immigration.” But the regular seating at the American Airlines Center is a different story: some sections are quite full, others have lots of empty seats (some occupied only by Stars and Stripes signs). The “nosebleeds” at the top seem completely unfilled so far. Of course, it’s still early days: Trump and other big name speakers are yet to appear. The stadium may well be much nearer capacity when they do. Chris Daniel, 44, from Houston, Texas, who has been a delegate to every Republican convention since 2004, said: “It feels different only because this is the midterms and we haven’t seen anything remotely like this since the 1800s. In this case, it is to rally the troops and get everyone on the same page so that we move forward towards November.” Trump merchandise is on sale in the square outside. It includes “Trump 2028” baseball caps. Reporting from Dallas At the Republican convention, several people – not me – are already on the booze. Miller Lite appears to be the beer of choice. Others have been taking advantage of free food provided by Steak n’ Shake, a burger company which has aligned itself with Robert F Kennedy’s idiosyncratic healthcare agenda. Steak n’ Shake has a van here with an inflatable box of fries which declare that its fries are “100% beef tallow” and do not contain seed oils. On a chalkboard on the side of the van someone has written “Eat mor bef tallow”. There are always interesting outfits at Republican conventions, and this year’s theme seems to be “sequins”. Among those sporting the style was Denise Hopkins, a keen Trump supporter from Louisiana who had an interesting idea about who should be the Republican nominee in 2028. “I would like President Trump. I think he’s doing a great job. I know he’s got family and grandkids, and he’s done so much for us, but if he would like to,” she said. The back of Hopkins’ jacket spelled out “Team Jesus” in sequins. It had a biblical verse at the bottom, but some of the sequins had fallen off, rendering it unreadable. Reporting from Dallas Ray Washburne, co-chair of the Republican midterm convention, has acknowledged that Donald Trump will be “front and center” of the event and denied the US president will be a liability for the party’s candidates. “Absolutely, he’s an asset – just look at the turnouts he gets,” Washburne told a roundtable at Bloomberg News in Dallas. “The ratings for listening to him speak will be fantastic because people want to hear what he’s got to say and he’s gonna set the tone for the rest of this fall. People are gonna look at that and his tone towards people like Ken Paxton and others to get the enthusiasm behind their campaigns.” Washburne said the two main contenders to host Republicans’ first midterm convention had been Dallas and Las Vegas. After Dallas got the nod in mid-June, the host committee raised $45m in three weeks as it raced to meet the September deadline. He expects an attendance of 18,000 to 20,000 each night in the American Airlines Center but is not aware of how many members of Congress will be among them. More than 1,600 reporters have been credentialed. Washburne, chair of the gas company Sunoco and vice-chair of Gillon Capital, said the idea of a midterm convention appealed to Trump. “He’s an entertainer. webTitle: Missouri’s voting maps saga reaches supreme court after conflicting rulings

fields.headline: Missouri’s voting maps saga reaches supreme court after conflicting rulings
fields.trailText: Appeal against approval of Trump-backed maps is latest move in legal back-and-forth spanning four courts
fields.bodyText: A high-stakes legal battle over Missouri’s congressional map returned on Wednesday to the US supreme court, after a series of conflicting decisions threw the state’s elections into turmoil less than two months before the November midterm elections. On Wednesday, a federal appeals court panel declined to block a ruling ordering Missouri to use the newly drawn congressional lines backed by Donald Trump to give Republicans an edge in the midterms elections. Opponents of the state’s redistricted map immediately filed an appeal to the US supreme court. The appeal is the latest move in an extraordinary legal back-and-forth spanning four courts. The rulings have left voters and local election officials in the state confused and uncertain about what the November ballot will look like. And there’s little time left before the pivotal elections that will decide which party controls a closely divided Congress – and will affect the fate of Trump’s agenda for the rest of his term. On Tuesday, the conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh had denied a request from Missouri officials to use the House map favored by Republicans. His refusal left in place a unanimous ruling from the Missouri supreme court, which blocked the newer maps, drawn to carve an additional Republican-friendly House seat. But not long after, a federal district judge in St Louis issued a contradictory decision, temporarily preventing the state from using its old congressional maps in the November elections. The temporary restraining order, or TRO, ordered Missouri to use the newly drawn districts that favor Republicans, which the state used in its August primary elections. That ruling, issued by Stephen Clark of the eastern district of Missouri, was then appealed to the eighth US circuit court of appeals. “Using a different map for the general election would wreak havoc on the fairness and orderliness of Missouri’s congressional elections, calling into question the candidacy of those nominated in the primaries and the votes of those who voted in the primaries. Widespread voter confusion would inevitably follow,” Clark, who was appointed by the president, wrote. “The public interest factor thus weighs in favor of a TRO.” People Not Politicians, the group leading the challenge to the Republican-drawn map in Missouri, said in a statement on Wednesday that the eighth circuit court’s decision to deny their stay request had left state election officials with “no legal map to use”. Trump urged Republican-led states last year to redraw congressional districts to their advantage ahead of November’s midterms, sparking a national redistricting battle. Texas went first, followed by Missouri in responding to the president’s push. The revised map, passed by state lawmakers last September, targeted the fifth congressional district held by Emanuel Cleaver of Kansas City, a longtime Democratic representative. It reassigned parts of Kansas City to two neighboring districts represented by Republicans and stretched the remainder of Cleaver’s district far eastward into rural Republican areas.
